lessons.title: Networking Fundamentals
lessons.concept: A computer network connects devices to share data and resources. Key elements include nodes (hosts/devices), links, protocols (rules for communication), and addressing (identifying devices). Networks can be classified by scale such as LAN (local) and WAN (wide area).
lessons.formula: Communication requires: sender + receiver + medium + message + protocol + addressing.
lessons.worked_example: In an office LAN, computers connect via switches and use protocols like Ethernet/IP to exchange files and access shared printers within the same local network.
mistakes: Confusing a protocol with a physical device
Assuming LAN and WAN differ only by speed (they primarily differ by geographic scope/ownership/technology)
Mixing up the roles of addressing and routing

lessons.title: OSI and TCP/IP Layered Models
lessons.concept: Layered models organize networking functions. The OSI model has 7 layers (Physical to Application) as a conceptual reference. The TCP/IP model has practical layers (Link/Network/Internet, Internet, Transport, Application in common descriptions) used on the Internet. Each layer provides services to the layer above and uses services below.
lessons.formula: OSI (top to bottom): Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical. TCP/IP common view: Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access/Link.
lessons.worked_example: When loading a web page, the application layer uses HTTP/HTTPS, transport layer uses TCP for reliable delivery, internet layer uses IP for addressing/routing, and link/physical layers handle local transmission over Wi-Fi/Ethernet.
mistakes: Memorizing layer names without associating basic responsibilities
Confusing transport-layer responsibilities (TCP/UDP) with network-layer responsibilities (IP routing)
Assuming OSI and TCP/IP layer counts map one-to-one in all representations

lessons.title: Common Protocols and Addressing Basics
lessons.concept: IP addresses identify devices on networks; IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses commonly written in dotted decimal form. DNS maps human-readable names to IP addresses. HTTP/HTTPS are application protocols for web communication; TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery while UDP is connectionless with lower overhead.
lessons.formula: DNS: name -> IP. TCP: reliable/ordered. UDP: connectionless/best-effort. IP: logical addressing and routing.
lessons.worked_example: Typing a URL triggers DNS to resolve the domain to an IP address. The browser then uses HTTPS over TCP to request the page from the server at that IP.
mistakes: Thinking DNS is used to assign MAC addresses (it resolves names to IPs)
Assuming UDP guarantees delivery/order like TCP
Confusing IP addresses (logical, network layer) with MAC addresses (link layer)
